newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - Surging zinc to lure Chinese sellers.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Surging zinc to lure Chinese sellers.

text.p: Sharply rising zinc prices may prove an irresistible lure for Chinese sellers to cash in and send the metal to Singapore warehouses, traders said on Friday.
Zinc hit a two-year peak of US$1,228 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Thursday before settling at $1,221, within striking distance of the January 1995 peak of $1,239.
"I would expect to see more zinc coming this way," the managing director of a European metal trading house told Reuters. "These prices are becoming very attractive for sellers."
"Good Far Eastern selling was seen at these levels," broker Brandeis said in its daily market review on Thursday.
Singapore-based metal traders estimate that up to 10,000 tonnes of zinc remain off-warrant here. Most of the material was shipped from China.
"I heard that some more Chinese zinc is supposed to be on its way here," a senior trader for a Japanese metal trading firm said. "But the precise amounts are not really clear."
Most traders said reports that some 20,000 tonnes of zinc from Chinese producers were sent to Singapore warehouses seem to be on the high side.
The volume of zinc on warrant in the LME warehouse here touched 5,200 tonnes on Tuesday, unchanged from last Friday's LME stocks report.

An official for a zinc supplier said the recent rise, while partly caused by speculative and fund-based buying, was not surprising because stocks are becoming tight, especially going into the second half of 1997.
Analysts estimate a shortfall in global supply of 250,000 tonnes for 1997.
"This price rise is not some freak. We're sold out on zinc. We've had to turn customers away," the official said, adding a price of $1,500 a tonne on the LME in coming weeks is not far-fetched.
"Our viewpoint is that this is just a continuation of the strong uptrend we will see in zinc this year," he added.
The rest of the Asian base metal trade was quiet, except for some aluminium buying by Japanese companies snapping up material for their second quarter requirements, dealers said.
"We saw some big quantity buying of a sizable number of ingots by Japanese companies for the second quarter," an aluminium dealer for a Japanese trading house said.
There were also some inquiries for small amounts of copper and lead, but most players were still out and will not be back in their offices until Monday.
Many had taken a long leave for the Chinese Lunar New Year, which was celebrated on February 7 and 8.
In copper, Far East traders expect three month prices on the LME to remain strong with a challenge to the $2,300 a tonne level seen in the near term.
"I think it may test $2,300 before profit-taking sets in," one chartist for a Singapore-based trading house said.
"I believe it will go past $2,300 soon and it may eventually test $2,400," a Japanese trader said.
Cash copper was being quoted by regional dealers here at around $2,380 a tonne against last week's level of $2,368. The backwardation was put at around $105.
Singapore copper premiums have risen to around $20-$30 a tonne, on the back of slightly firmer demand, dealers said.
"There's some interest in copper at the moment and that helped nudge premiums up," one said. "But physical buying remains light."
